Albin Mehmeti graduated in Architecture at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL, Master of Science in Architecture).

He worked at Seyler & Lucan architectes-urbanistes in Paris, where he addressed the housing question through typological studies.

He contributed to teaching programs at EPFL, collaborating with Jo Taillieu and Nicola Braghieri.

Albin is also active in painting architecture.

Alexander Wegener graduated in Architecture at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL) and at the Accademia di Architettura di Mendrisio.

He contributed to publications of Office Without Office.

He worked at OFFICE KGDVS in Brussels, focusing on form and its relationship to the city, and at Studio Paola Viganò, contributing to research on socio-ecological transition in the Grand Genève context.

*Adolf Loos, architecte des pauvres* examines how housing became central in Loos’ work.

It explores how villa spatial strategies inform collective housing.

In rural contexts, Loos develops a sequence of autonomous spaces forming a *raumplan*.

In the urban context of Vienna, this transforms into a continuous ground condition.

This becomes a mechanism structuring both the building and social relationships.

The work ultimately proposes a new condition of *urban domesticity*.

Before the Swiss Box engages with a specific period in the work of *Herzog & de Meuron* between 1984 and 1987.

Rather than reinforcing the “Swiss box” identity, it examines its origins.

It highlights projects of varying scales that share a common attitude toward the city.

Through layers of diffusion and dissimulation, architectural harshness softens and engages context.

The work proposes an alternative reading of Swiss architectural identity.

While today’s condition of architecture is faced with the question of reuse, addressing existing structures opens a field for experimentation.

This condition risks reducing architecture to constrained decisions, where form becomes either abstract or diminished.

Historical precedents such as Bramante’s Tempietto or Terragni’s “Biological Pillar” offer pragmatic responses.

However, by integrating reuse as one element among others, they often dissolve the tension of the project.

Rather than seeking freedom within limitation, incompleteness becomes a positive argument for form to question its boundaries.

The “Colonne-cadre” explores this condition, rethinking the relation between project and context.

Developed in research on the Lemanic arc, it reveals spatial potential through transformation.

It becomes a principle for a composite construction, proposing new typological and spatial relationships.

In the last year of architecture studies at the *Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne*, students undertake a research called *énoncé théorique*.

This task opens questions about the role of research in architecture and its possible forms.

It introduces writing as one tool among others within the architectural project.

Standing between education and practice, these texts operate within a degree of abstraction.

They aim to define a shared knowledge as cultural common ground.

Rather than a support for argument, text is understood as a specific tool with its own rules.

It allows research to be undertaken with *conviction, passion and precision*.

The book presents a double portrait: on one side we have *Manfredo Tafuri* offering critical tools to approach contemporaneity.

On the other, fragments of *Le Corbusier* are used to observe their resolution into architectural form.

*Open Hand Open Castle* compiles notes forming an argument on ideology and form.

It seeks to establish a new relationship between the *chose humaine*, the social stance, and architectural culture.

Aldo Rossi’s work, as well-known as it is, as mysterious as it remains, has plenty to deliver yet again to the architectural debate, for it is highly theoretical without becoming a *theory* on its own.

*Architecture for museums* (1966) and *A Scientific Autobiography* (1981) represent a difficult pairing where the architect’s final call seems to have turned into the distant memory of its predecessor.

And as remembering is to love again, these two texts remain deeply related to each other.

They best represent the architect’s work, his factual *attempt* at the making of architecture. In that sense, the architectural project is the series rather than a project.

Writing remains the ultimate proof of an incomplete architecture if only *realized* in the physical world.

Thus, the architectural project might become the description of its own project.

By engaging with Rossi’s insistence on certain seemingly *vague* themes, the essay elaborates on the need for architects to refer to something *external*.

Reading Rossi’s *Scientific Autobiography* evokes a sense of unease, as one steps into the architect’s intimate world.

To remember is to love again.
